title: Sitagliptin: DPP-4 Therapy With Renal and Pancreatitis Awareness
bottomLine: Sitagliptin is a DPP-4 inhibitor for type 2 diabetes that increases incretin activity. It has low intrinsic hypoglycemia risk but requires renal-dose awareness and monitoring for pancreatitis, severe joint pain, heart-failure symptoms, hypersensitivity, and bullous pemphigoid.
recognize: Persistent severe abdominal pain can signal pancreatitis.
Hypoglycemia risk rises when combined with insulin or insulin secretagogues.
priorities: Review renal function and the complete glucose-lowering regimen.
Escalate pancreatitis symptoms, severe hypersensitivity, blistering skin disease, or new/worsening heart-failure symptoms.
assessMonitor: Monitor glucose/A1C trend, renal function, abdominal symptoms, hypoglycemia, edema/dyspnea, and skin findings.
interventions: Administer consistently and reinforce that medication complements nutrition/activity and monitoring plans.
medicationSafety: Dose adjustment is required for reduced renal function according to current labeling.
Not treatment for type 1 diabetes or DKA.
teaching: Report severe abdominal pain, blistering rash, swelling, or new shortness of breath promptly.
delegationScope: PNs may administer and monitor; medication selection/dose adjustment remains prescriber-directed.
examTrap: Assuming a low-hypoglycemia drug can never contribute to hypoglycemia when combined with insulin.
oneLinePearl: Sitagliptin is gentle on glucose lows—but kidneys, pancreas, skin, and heart still matter.

title: Linagliptin: DPP-4 Therapy With Minimal Renal Dose Adjustment
bottomLine: Linagliptin is a DPP-4 inhibitor for type 2 diabetes. Unlike many agents in the class, routine renal dose adjustment is generally not required, but pancreatitis, hypersensitivity, severe joint pain, bullous pemphigoid, and combination-therapy hypoglycemia remain relevant.
recognize: Do not generalize renal-dose rules from sitagliptin to linagliptin.
Hypoglycemia is more likely when used with insulin or a secretagogue.
priorities: Verify the exact DPP-4 inhibitor and complete diabetes regimen.
Escalate pancreatitis symptoms, serious rash/blisters, or angioedema.
assessMonitor: Monitor glucose trend, abdominal symptoms, skin findings, hypersensitivity, and hypoglycemia.
interventions: Administer consistently and reinforce product-specific instructions rather than class assumptions.
medicationSafety: Not indicated for type 1 diabetes or DKA.
Strong P-gp/CYP3A4 inducers can reduce exposure; review interactions.
teaching: Know the exact drug name; renal instructions and interactions differ within the DPP-4 class.
delegationScope: PNs may administer and monitor; treatment changes require prescriber review.
examTrap: Automatically reducing linagliptin because another DPP-4 inhibitor required renal adjustment.
oneLinePearl: Same class does not mean same renal rule.

title: Pioglitazone: Insulin Sensitization With a Heart-Failure Boxed Warning
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Pioglitazone is a thiazolidinedione that improves insulin sensitivity but can cause or worsen congestive heart failure through fluid retention. Weight gain, edema, fractures, macular edema, hepatic issues, and bladder-tumor history also matter.
recognize: Rapid weight gain, edema, orthopnea, or dyspnea may signal fluid retention/heart failure.
It does not provide rapid correction of severe hyperglycemia.
priorities: Review heart-failure status, edema/weight, liver history, fracture risk, and bladder-cancer history.
Escalate new/worsening dyspnea, edema, or rapid weight gain.
assessMonitor: Monitor weight, edema, respiratory symptoms, glucose/A1C, liver symptoms, vision change, and fracture risk.
interventions: Administer as prescribed and reinforce daily monitoring for fluid-retention symptoms when at risk.
medicationSafety: Current labeling carries a boxed warning for congestive heart failure.
Avoid initiation in severe symptomatic heart failure per labeling.
teaching: Report swelling, rapid weight gain, shortness of breath, or vision changes promptly.
delegationScope: PNs may administer and monitor; heart-failure deterioration requires escalation.
examTrap: Reassuring a patient that new edema is expected and harmless because the glucose is improving.
oneLinePearl: Pioglitazone improves insulin sensitivity but can worsen the fluid-sensitive heart.

title: Acarbose: Postprandial Glucose Control and the Dextrose Hypoglycemia Rule
bottomLine: Acarbose inhibits intestinal alpha-glucosidase to slow carbohydrate digestion and blunt postprandial glucose rise. It must be taken with the first bite of meals; gas/diarrhea are common, and hypoglycemia from combination therapy should be treated with glucose/dextrose rather than relying on sucrose digestion.
recognize: Flatulence, abdominal discomfort, and diarrhea are mechanism-related effects.
Acarbose alone rarely causes hypoglycemia, but combination therapy can.
priorities: Verify meal timing and concurrent insulin/secretagogue use.
Assess significant GI disease or obstruction risk and hepatic context.
assessMonitor: Monitor postprandial glucose/A1C, GI tolerance, hypoglycemia, and liver tests when ordered.
interventions: Give with the first bite of each main meal.
medicationSafety: If hypoglycemia occurs while acarbose is active, use oral glucose/dextrose when the patient can safely swallow rather than table sugar alone.
Avoid in significant intestinal obstruction/inflammatory bowel conditions listed in labeling.
teaching: Take with the first bite of food and keep a glucose source available if other diabetes drugs can cause lows.
delegationScope: PNs may administer and monitor; severe GI or glycemic deterioration requires escalation.
examTrap: Treating combination-therapy hypoglycemia with sucrose candy and expecting normal digestion despite alpha-glucosidase blockade.
oneLinePearl: Acarbose acts at the first bite—and hypoglycemia needs glucose, not delayed sucrose digestion.

title: Insulin Glargine: Basal Coverage and Concentration Safety
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Insulin glargine provides long-acting basal insulin coverage; it does not replace rapid-acting mealtime or acute DKA insulin when those are required. Hypoglycemia, hypokalemia, product concentration/device confusion, and unsafe mixing are major administration risks.
recognize: Basal insulin continues to cover fasting hepatic glucose production even when a patient is not eating.
Different glargine products/concentrations are not safely converted by guesswork.
priorities: Verify exact product, concentration, dose, device, glucose trend, nutrition status, and renal function.
Escalate recurrent hypoglycemia or unclear substitution/concentration orders before administration.
assessMonitor: Monitor glucose, hypoglycemia symptoms, potassium when clinically indicated, injection sites, nutrition changes, and renal function.
interventions: Administer subcutaneously using the correct device and rotate injection sites.
medicationSafety: Do not mix or dilute insulin glargine unless the exact product label explicitly permits it; standard glargine products are generally administered separately.
Never transfer pen insulin into a syringe unless product instructions specifically authorize it.
teaching: Know the exact insulin name/concentration, use a new needle as directed, rotate sites, and never share pens.
delegationScope: Insulin administration authority varies by setting/state; PN must follow facility verification policy and escalate unclear orders.
examTrap: Holding all basal insulin solely because the patient is NPO without checking the prescribed diabetes plan.
oneLinePearl: Glargine is background insulin—verify the exact concentration before every dose.
sourceBasis: DailyMed insulin glargine labeling current 2026 including Langlara

title: Insulin Lispro: Rapid Meal Coverage and Intake Matching
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Insulin lispro is rapid-acting insulin used for mealtime and correction coverage. Safe administration requires matching dose timing to actual food availability/intake, verifying concentration/device, and monitoring for hypoglycemia and potassium shifts.
recognize: A delayed or missed meal after lispro can rapidly produce hypoglycemia.
U-100 and U-200 products/devices require exact verification.
priorities: Confirm glucose, ordered dose, actual meal availability, product concentration, and ability to eat before administration.
Escalate uncertain intake or concentration mismatch rather than guessing.
assessMonitor: Monitor glucose response, hypoglycemia, meal intake, potassium when clinically indicated, and injection sites.
interventions: Coordinate administration closely with meals according to the exact product/order.
medicationSafety: Route permissions differ by formulation; do not assume every lispro product can be administered IV.
Do not withdraw concentrated pen insulin into a syringe.
teaching: Carry a rapid glucose source, match insulin to meals as taught, and verify the pen label each time.
delegationScope: PN insulin authority varies by state/facility; follow independent-check and meal-coordination policies.
examTrap: Giving rapid-acting insulin because the tray is 'on the way' when the patient may not actually receive or tolerate food.
oneLinePearl: Lispro moves fast—food must be real, not hypothetical.

title: Nasal Glucagon: Severe Hypoglycemia Rescue Without Inhalation
bottomLine: Intranasal glucagon is emergency rescue for severe hypoglycemia when the patient cannot safely take oral carbohydrate. It is absorbed through the nasal mucosa and does not require the patient to inhale; emergency follow-up and carbohydrate replacement after recovery remain essential.
recognize: Severe hypoglycemia may cause confusion, seizure, or unconsciousness.
Nausea/vomiting may occur after glucagon, creating aspiration risk.
priorities: Give rescue glucagon promptly per product instructions when indicated and activate emergency help.
Protect the airway/position safely and recheck glucose/response.
assessMonitor: Monitor consciousness, airway/breathing, glucose response, vomiting, and recurrence.
interventions: Administer the single-use nasal device as directed; once awake and able to swallow, provide oral carbohydrate per plan.
medicationSafety: The patient does not need to inhale or sniff the dose.
Contraindicated in pheochromocytoma and insulinoma because glucagon can provoke dangerous responses.
teaching: Caregivers should know where the device is, how to use it, and that emergency help is still needed after administration.
delegationScope: Emergency glucagon administration may be allowed under protocols; scope varies by setting/state and severe hypoglycemia requires immediate escalation.
examTrap: Waiting for an unconscious patient to inhale through the nose before giving nasal glucagon.
oneLinePearl: Nasal glucagon does not need a breath—it needs rapid action and follow-up.

title: Cabergoline: Hyperprolactinemia Therapy With Valvular and Fibrotic Screening
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Cabergoline is a dopamine-receptor agonist used for adult hyperprolactinemic disorders. Current labeling requires evaluation for valvular heart disease before therapy and highlights valvular/fibrotic disease, orthostasis, and impulse-control behaviors; it should not be used simply to suppress normal postpartum lactation.
recognize: Dyspnea, persistent cough, edema, flank/back pain, or new murmur can suggest fibrotic/valvular complications.
Compulsive gambling, spending, eating, or sexual behavior can be medication related.
priorities: Verify baseline valvular evaluation/echo and indication.
Escalate cardiopulmonary/fibrotic symptoms, syncope, or major impulse-control change.
assessMonitor: Monitor prolactin response, BP/orthostasis, cardiac/fibrotic symptoms, behavior, and pregnancy status when relevant.
interventions: Administer as prescribed and reinforce slow position changes.
medicationSafety: D2 antagonists can oppose cabergoline's effect.
Current labeling advises avoiding cabergoline for suppression of physiologic postpartum lactation because of serious adverse-reaction risk.
teaching: Report breathing problems, swelling, fainting, or new compulsive behaviors.
delegationScope: PNs may administer and monitor; diagnostic echo/prolactin treatment decisions remain prescriber-directed.
examTrap: Using cabergoline routinely to stop normal postpartum lactation without recognizing the label warning.
oneLinePearl: Cabergoline lowers prolactin, but screen the valves and watch for fibrosis and impulse changes.

title: Bromocriptine: Dopamine Agonism Across Prolactin and Parkinson Indications
bottomLine: Bromocriptine is an ergot-derived dopamine agonist used in selected hyperprolactinemia, Parkinson, acromegaly, and formulation-specific metabolic indications. Orthostasis, nausea, hallucinations, somnolence, and drug interactions require careful indication/formulation verification.
recognize: Dizziness and orthostatic symptoms are common early/titration effects.
Hallucinations or excessive sleepiness may be more prominent in neurologic use.
priorities: Verify exact formulation and indication because bromocriptine products are not interchangeable by assumption.
Review D2-antagonist drugs and cardiovascular/psychiatric risk.
assessMonitor: Monitor BP/orthostasis, nausea, mental status, sleepiness, therapeutic response, and interaction profile.
interventions: Administer with food when directed to reduce GI intolerance and use fall precautions during titration.
medicationSafety: Dopamine antagonists can reduce therapeutic effect.
Do not use legacy postpartum lactation-suppression assumptions without current product-specific indication and prescriber review.
redFlags: Chest pain or major neurologic symptoms
teaching: Rise slowly and report hallucinations, fainting, or severe daytime sleepiness.
delegationScope: PNs may administer and monitor; indication/formulation and dose changes remain prescriber-directed.
examTrap: Treating every bromocriptine formulation as the same drug schedule for every indication.
oneLinePearl: With bromocriptine, first verify which formulation and why the patient takes it.

title: Somatropin: Growth Hormone Replacement and Pediatric Growth Safety
bottomLine: Somatropin is recombinant human growth hormone used for specific pediatric growth disorders and adult growth-hormone deficiency, not nonspecific short stature or performance enhancement. Glucose intolerance, intracranial hypertension, slipped capital femoral epiphysis, edema, thyroid/adrenal interactions, and product-specific injection technique require monitoring.
recognize: New limp, hip/knee pain, or reduced hip motion in a growing child can indicate slipped capital femoral epiphysis.
Headache, visual change, nausea, or vomiting can signal intracranial hypertension.
priorities: Verify the exact indication/product and endocrine monitoring plan.
Escalate new limp/hip pain, severe headache/vision symptoms, or adrenal-insufficiency signs.
assessMonitor: Monitor growth response/IGF-related plan, glucose, thyroid function, edema, injection sites, headache/vision symptoms, gait/hip pain, and adrenal context.
interventions: Administer subcutaneously using the exact device/product instructions and rotate sites.
medicationSafety: Growth-hormone products have indication- and device-specific dosing; never convert cartridges/devices by guesswork.
Somatropin can unmask central hypothyroidism or hypoadrenalism and can worsen glucose intolerance.
teaching: Report new limp/hip pain, severe headaches/vision changes, swelling, or excessive thirst/urination; use only the prescribed product/device.
delegationScope: PNs may administer and reinforce injection teaching where authorized; growth-hormone diagnosis/dose titration remains specialist/prescriber-directed.
examTrap: Dismissing a new limp in a child on growth hormone as ordinary growing pains.
oneLinePearl: Growth hormone accelerates growth—watch the head, hips, glucose, thyroid, and adrenal axis.
sourceBasis: DailyMed HUMATROPE somatropin labeling with 2025 slipped-capital-femoral-epiphysis update
